extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office examiners, patent attorneys, and other practitioners applying MPEP obviousness guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness of claimed chemical/genus-species inventions, including how to analyze prior art genera/species, structural similarity (homologs/isomers), motivation to select claimed species, predictability, and applicant rebuttal evidence. Oriented to examination practice under the MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings regarding the structure of a disclosed prior art genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should make findings as to the structure of the disclosed prior art genus and that of any expressly described species or subgenus within the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the structural features of the genus and any exemplified species/subgenera. Compare structural elements explicitly to support later selection/expectation analyses (see MPEP § 2144.08).

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings regarding properties, utilities, and limitations of the prior art genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should make findings as to any physical or chemical properties and utilities disclosed for the genus, as well as any suggested limitations on the usefulness of the genus, and any problems alleged to be addressed by the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document disclosed utilities, known problems, and any language in the reference that limits usefulness — these inform motivation and whether the prior art would prompt selection of a claimed species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings regarding predictability of the technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should make findings as to the predictability of the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the field is predictable (where structural similarity reasonably suggests similar properties) or unpredictable (where structural similarity may not imply similar function). Case examples: Dillon, May, Schechter, O’Farrell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings regarding the number of species encompassed by the genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should make findings as to the number of species encompassed by the genus taking into consideration all of the variables possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider genus size and the number of meaningful permutations; a very small, limited genus may make envisioning each member reasonable (e.g., Petering) while a large diverse genus may not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare claimed species to the closest disclosed prior art species/subgenus
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the structure of the disclosed genus and any expressly described species/subgenus are identified, Office personnel should compare them to the claimed species/subgenus to determine the differences and identify the closest disclosed species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit findings on similarities and differences including structure, properties, and utilities; identify the closest prior art species of record and analyze whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious (see Stratoflex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should evaluate the prior art from the standpoint of the hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art at the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve level of skill to maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry. Facts of record about skill are commonly found in the prior art; consider applicant evidence as appropriate (see Ryko, Uniroyal, MPEP §§2141, 2141.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether one of ordinary skill would have been motivated to select the claimed species/subgenus
rubrics_metrics.description: In light of Graham factors, determine whether it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill to make the claimed invention as a whole, i.e., to select the claimed species or subgenus from the disclosed prior art genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the totality of prior art teachings and make factual findings articulating what teachings or suggestions would have motivated selection. See Kulling, Panduit, and ensure findings support a prima facie case before concluding obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the size of the genus as a motive factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the size of the prior art genus, bearing in mind that size alone cannot support an obviousness rejection; however, a genus may be so small that it would anticipate the claimed species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply a per se rule; evaluate ‘total circumstances’ including number of permissible variations. Small, narrowly varying genera (e.g., Petering) can render selection foreseeable; large diverse genera may not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider any express teachings in the prior art that teach selecting the claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art reference expressly teaches a particular reason to select the claimed species or subgenus, point out the express disclosure and explain why it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to select the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit statements (including expressed equivalences or references between documents) that would have motivated selection or combination (see Merck v. Biocraft, In re Kemps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider teachings of structural similarity (typical/preferred species)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any teachings of a 'typical', 'preferred', or 'optimum' species or subgenus within the disclosed genus; if such species is structurally similar to the claimed species, its disclosure may provide a reason to choose the claimed species based on expectation of similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural relationships (homologs, adjacent homologs, isomers, stereoisomers, etc.) can suggest motivation to select claimed compounds because similar structure often implies similar properties (see Dillon, Deuel, and examples cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider teachings of similar properties or uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any teachings that the prior art species or subgenus possess properties or utilities similar to those claimed; properties/utilities provide real-world motivation to make structurally similar species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of similar utilities weighs in favor of obviousness; lack of useful properties in the prior art weighs against motivation. Very close structural similarity plus similar utilities can make a prima facie case (see Dillon, Stemniski, Grabiak).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the predictability of the technology when assessing motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the predictability of the technology: if the technology is unpredictable, structurally similar species are less likely to render a claimed species obvious because properties may not be inferred from structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a reasonable expectation of success exists (obviousness requires reasonable expectation, not absolute predictability). Use case law examples (Dillon, May, Schechter, O’Farrell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider any other teachings or totality of evidence that support selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond enumerated categories, consider the totality of relevant teachings in the prior art; other, unusual relevant teachings may support selection of the species/subgenus and a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to atypical but case-specific teachings; do not limit analysis to a fixed checklist — treat evidence holistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors and specifically articulate what teachings or suggestions in the prior art would have motivated one of ordinary skill to select the claimed species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly tie fact-findings to motivation and assess whether those findings, considered as a whole, support a prima facie case of obviousness. Cite precedent (Kulling, Panduit) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness rejection based on close structural similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be made when chemical compounds have very close structural similarities and similar utilities; the rejection is founded on the expectation that compounds similar in structure will have similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structural-and-functional similarity to establish motivation to make a claimed compound in expectation of similar properties (see In re Payne, Papesch, Dillon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for homology and isomerism as facts (not conclusive) in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Homology and isomerism are facts which must be considered with all other relevant facts in determining obviousness; such relationships often create a presumption of similar properties but are not automatically dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position isomers, homologs, stereoisomers often carry a presumption of similar properties, but divergent homologs or isomers may not. View claims and references 'as a whole' (see Wilder, May, Mills, Langer).

rubrics_metrics.name: True homologous or isomeric relationship is not required to render obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a true homologous or isomeric relationship is not controlling — prior art structures need not be true homologs/isomers to render structurally similar compounds prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show structural similarity short of formal homology/isomerism can still motivate selection if similarity and properties are sufficiently close (see Payne, Dillon, Merck).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether the prior art teaches a method for making the claimed compound
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence—or absence—of a suitably operative, obvious process for making a composition of matter may have an ultimate bearing on whether that composition is obvious (i.e., lack of a method may overcome presumption of obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making the claimed compound at the relevant time, it may be improper to conclude the compound was in the public's possession. Consider Maloney, Hoeksema and related authority; methodology can be central depending on facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of obviousness may be overcome where there is no reasonable expectation of similar properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption of obviousness based on a reference disclosing structurally similar compounds may be overcome where there is evidence showing there is no reasonable expectation of similar properties in structurally similar compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence demonstrating unpredictability or that structurally similar compounds lack shared properties can rebut prima facie obviousness (see May, Schechter, Ex parte Blattner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art compounds lacking utility or disclosed only as intermediates may not render claimed compounds obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art does not teach any specific or significant utility for the disclosed compounds, or only discloses them as intermediates, then structurally similar claimed compounds may not be prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of disclosed utility undermines motivation to make related compounds; intermediates shown only as synthesis steps are unlikely to be investigated for other utilities (see Stemniski, Albrecht, Lalu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness rebuttable by evidence of unexpected results and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness based on structural similarity is rebuttable by proof that the claimed compounds possess unexpectedly advantageous or superior properties and by secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, copying, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence must be factual (data, declarations, comparative results); arguments alone are insufficient. Consider types of rebuttal: unexpected results, commercial success, copying, expert declarations on level of skill/state of art, and evidence that no method of making was known (see Papesch, Soni, Piasecki, Dillon, Mayne, GPAC, Hybritech). Ensure comparisons are supported by evidence, not conclusory statements.
